claim: Transcription initiation is the first and most highly regulated step in gene expression.
source: Transcription initiation is the first and most highly regulated step in gene expression (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Ruff et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Ruff et al., 2015).

claim: During transcription initiation, RNA polymerase (RNAP), together with the transcription initiation factor σ, unwinds ~13 bp of promoter DNA to form a 'transcription bubble'.
source: During transcription initiation, RNA polymerase (RNAP), together with the transcription initiation factor σ, unwinds ~13 bp of promoter DNA to form a 'transcription bubble', and places the template-strand ssDNA of the unwound transcription bubble in contact with the RNAP active centre, yielding a catalytically competent RNAP-promoter transcription-initiation complex (RPo; Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019).

claim: High-resolution structures of RPo define the contacts that RNAP and σ make with promoter DNA, as well as the conformation and interactions of unwound template-strand ssDNA engaging the RNAP active centre.
source: High-resolution structures of RPo define the contacts that RNAP and σ make with promoter DNA, as well as the conformation and interactions of unwound template-strand ssDNA engaging the RNAP active centre (Bae et al., 2015; Zuo and Steitz, 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Bae et al., 2015; Zuo and Steitz, 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: Transcription-bubble formation is initiated by unwinding the DNA base pair at the upstream end of the transcription bubble.
source: Structural and biochemical experiments suggest that transcription-bubble formation is initiated by unwinding the DNA base pair at the upstream end of the transcription bubble – breaking the base pair, and unstacking and flipping the non-template-strand base of the broken base pair, and inserting the unstacked and flipped non-template-strand base into a protein pocket of σ – followed by propagation of the unwinding in a downstream direction (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Ruff et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012; Feklistov and Darst, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural and biochemical experiments (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Ruff et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012; Feklistov and Darst, 2011).

claim: In crystal structures of RNAP σ holoenzyme, the RNAP active-centre cleft is too narrow to accommodate double-stranded DNA (<20 Å).
source: In crystal structures of RNAP σ holoenzyme, the RNAP active-centre cleft is too narrow to accommodate double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) (<20 Å), and σ obstructs access of dsDNA to the RNAP active-centre cleft (Mekler et al., 2002; Murakami et al., 2002b; Murakami et al., 2002a; Vassylyev et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to crystal structures (Mekler et al., 2002; Murakami et al., 2002b; Murakami et al., 2002a; Vassylyev et al., 2002).

claim: There is no unobstructed path by which dsDNA can access the RNAP active-centre cleft in RNAP holoenzyme.
source: As a result, there is no unobstructed path by which dsDNA can access the RNAP active-centre cleft in RNAP holoenzyme (Mekler et al., 2002; Murakami et al., 2002b; Murakami et al., 2002a; Vassylyev et al., 2002; Young et al., 2002; Murakami and Darst, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Mekler et al., 2002; Murakami et al., 2002b; Murakami et al., 2002a; Vassylyev et al., 2002; Young et al., 2002; Murakami and Darst, 2003).

claim: 'Load-unwind' models propose that the RNAP active-centre cleft opens through the swinging outward of the clamp, allowing loading of promoter DNA into the active-centre cleft as dsDNA.
source: One class of models, termed 'load-unwind' models, propose that: (i) the RNAP active-centre cleft opens, through the swinging outward of one wall, termed the 'clamp', of the active-centre cleft, allowing loading of promoter DNA into the active-centre cleft as dsDNA; (ii) promoter DNA unwinds inside the active-centre cleft; and (iii) the active-centre cleft closes, through the swinging inward of the clamp, during or after DNA unwinding (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Ruff et al., 2015; Mekler et al., 2002; Murakami et al., 2002b; Murakami et al., 2002a; Young et al., 2002; Darst et al., 2002; Chakraborty et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim describes a model proposed in the literature, supported by citations (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Ruff et al., 2015; Mekler et al., 2002; Murakami et al., 2002b; Murakami et al., 2002a; Young et al., 2002; Darst et al., 2002; Chakraborty et al., 2012).

claim: 'Unwind-load' models propose that promoter DNA unwinds outside the RNAP active-centre cleft and unwound-promoter DNA loads into the active-centre cleft as single-stranded DNA.
source: The other class of models, termed 'unwind-load' models, proposes that: (i) promoter DNA unwinds outside the RNAP active-centre cleft and (ii) unwound-promoter DNA loads into the active-centre cleft as single-stranded DNA (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Vassylyev et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim describes a model proposed in the literature, supported by citations (Mazumder and Kapanidis, 2019; Vassylyev et al., 2002).

claim: A promoter derivative having Cy3 site-specifically incorporated in the transcription-bubble region exhibits an ~2-fold increase in fluorescence emission intensity upon promoter unwinding during RPo formation.
source: Previous work indicates that a promoter derivative having the fluorescent probe Cy3 site-specifically incorporated in the transcription-bubble region exhibits an ~2-fold increase in fluorescence emission intensity upon promoter unwinding during RPo formation and exhibits an ~ 2-fold decrease in fluorescence emission intensity upon promoter rewinding during promoter escape (Feklistov et al., 2017; Ko and Heyduk, 2014; Koh et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Feklistov et al., 2017; Ko and Heyduk, 2014; Koh et al., 2018).

claim: Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments bound exclusively to immobilised RNAP molecules.
source: Control experiments show that: (i) Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments bound exclusively to immobilised RNAP molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and the majority (~60%) of the resulting complexes were resistant to challenge with heparin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: The majority (~60%) of RNAP-promoter complexes were resistant to challenge with heparin.
source: Control experiments show that: (i) Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments bound exclusively to immobilised RNAP molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and the majority (~60%) of the resulting complexes were resistant to challenge with heparin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Binding of Cy3-containing non-promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP holoenzyme molecules did not result in heparin-resistant complexes.
source: (ii) binding of Cy3-containing non-promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP holoenzyme molecules did not result in heparin-resistant complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Binding of Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP core enzyme molecules did not result in heparin-resistant complexes.
source: (iii) binding of Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP core enzyme molecules did not result in heparin-resistant complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Sequence-specific, heparin-resistant, complexes were formed only between RNAP holoenzyme and Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments.
source: These results confirm that sequence-specific, heparin-resistant, complexes were formed only between RNAP holoenzyme and Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the control experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: A large class of trajectories (~45%) was characterised by the appearance of a fluorescence intensity of ~200 counts, followed by an increase in fluorescence intensity to ~450 counts.
source: A large class of trajectories (~45%) was characterised by the appearance of a fluorescence intensity of ~200 counts, followed by an increase in fluorescence intensity to ~450 counts, followed by either a decrease of the intensity to ~200 counts or a disappearance of the intensity (Figure 1B, top left; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Binding of Cy3-containing non-promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP holoenzyme did not result in ≥2-fold fluorescence enhancement.
source: Control experiments show that (i) binding of Cy3-containing non-promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP holoenzyme did not result in ≥2-fold fluorescence enhancement (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Binding of Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP core molecules did not result in ≥2-fold fluorescence enhancement events for the overwhelming majority of the time trajectories (~96%).
source: (ii) binding of Cy3-containing promoter DNA fragments to immobilised RNAP core molecules did not result in ≥2-fold fluorescence enhancement events for the overwhelming majority of the time trajectories (~96%; Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The detected ~2-fold fluorescence enhancement events represent sequence-specific complexes between RNAP holoenzyme and promoter DNA fragments.
source: These results indicate that the detected ~2-fold fluorescence enhancement events represent sequence-specific complexes between RNAP holoenzyme and promoter DNA fragments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the control experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Upon addition of an NTP subset enabling synthesis of transcripts up to 11 nt in length (ATP, UTP, and GTP), ~ 49% of trajectories showed formation of a stable unwound-promoter state.
source: Upon addition of an NTP subset enabling synthesis of transcripts up to 11 nt in length (ATP, UTP, and GTP), ~ 49% of trajectories showed formation of a stable unwound-promoter state (with fluorescence intensity similar to that of the sub-population exhibiting promoter unwinding), as expected for the formation of initial transcribing complexes (RPitc <11; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, top; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Upon subsequent addition of a separate NTP subset (GTP and CTP), enabling synthesis of transcripts up to 14 nt in length, ~ 27% of the resulting complexes showed formation of a stable rewound-promoter state.
source: Upon subsequent addition of a separate NTP subset (GTP and CTP), enabling synthesis of transcripts up to 14 nt in length, ~ 27% of the resulting complexes showed formation of a stable rewound-promoter state (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, bottom), as expected for promoter escape and formation of a transcription elongation complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: RNAP-promoter complexes formed in these experiments are transcriptionally active and are competent for promoter escape.
source: The results show that RNAP-promoter complexes formed in these experiments are transcriptionally active and are competent for promoter escape (see also Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing formation of initial transcribing complexes and promoter escape.

claim: The dwell-time histogram for lacCONS-[+2 Cy3] showed a peaked distribution, indicating a non-Markovian process having more than one rate-limiting steps before the formation of the unwound state.
source: The dwell-time histogram showed a peaked distribution, indicating a non-Markovian process having more than one rate-limiting steps before the formation of the unwound state (Floyd et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Floyd et al., 2010) and by the experimental data.

claim: The total time spent in the pre-unwinding state for lacCONS-[+2 Cy3] was estimated to be ~7.5 s.
source: We fitted this histogram to a two-exponential function (see Materials and methods for a detailed explanation; Floyd et al., 2010), and estimated the total time spent in the pre-unwinding state to be ~7.5 s (Figure 1B, top right; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1D.

claim: Time trajectories for pre-unwound lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] showed significantly shorter dwell times in the pre-unwinding state (~2.8 s vs. ~7.5 s).
source: Time trajectories for pre-unwound lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] were qualitatively similar to those for lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] in terms of the intensity increase (Figure 1B, middle left, S4A) and the shape of the dwell-time histogram (Figure 1B, middle right); however, the trajectories showed significantly shorter dwell times in the pre-unwinding state (~2.8 s vs. ~7.5 s; Figure 1B, middle right vs. top right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Time trajectories for G/C lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] showed significantly longer dwell times in the pre-unwinding state (~18.8 s vs. 7.5 s).
source: Time trajectories for G/C lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] showed significantly longer dwell times in the pre-unwinding state (~18.8 s vs. 7.5 s; Figure 1B, bottom right vs. top right; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1D.

claim: Dwell times in the pre-unwinding state depend on energy barriers for promoter unwinding.
source: Taken together, these results show that dwell times in the pre-unwinding state depend on energy barriers for promoter unwinding, consistent with expectation that the dwell times report on the kinetics of promoter unwinding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing different dwell times for promoters with different energy barriers.

claim: The dwell times in the pre-unwinding state for lacCONS-[–9 Cy3] were significantly shorter than for lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3]: ~ 5.5 s vs. ~7.5 s.
source: The resulting trajectories were similar in terms of intensity increases (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) and dwell-time-distribution shapes to those obtained with promoter DNA fragments having Cy3 incorporated in the downstream edge of the transcription bubble, but the dwell times in the pre-unwinding state were significantly shorter: ~ 5.5 s vs. ~7.5 s for lacCONS-[–9 Cy3] vs. lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] (Figure 1C, top right vs. Figure 1B, top right; Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, Figure 1B, and Figure 1D.

claim: The dwell times in the pre-unwinding state for G/C lacCONS-[–9 Cy3] were significantly shorter than for G/C lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3]: ~6.0 s vs. ~18.8 s.
source: and ~6.0 s vs. ~18.8 s for G/C lacCONS-[–9 Cy3] vs. G/C lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] (Figure 1C, bottom right vs. Figure 1B, bottom right; 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, Figure 1B, and Figure 1D.

claim: For the promoters analysed, unwinding of the upstream half of the transcription bubble occurs faster than unwinding of the downstream half of the transcription bubble.
source: We conclude that, for the promoters analysed, unwinding of the upstream half of the transcription bubble occurs faster than unwinding of the downstream half of the transcription bubble
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing shorter dwell times for upstream unwinding compared to total unwinding time.

claim: Promoter unwinding proceeds in a step-wise fashion, in an upstream-downstream direction.
source: Our results confirm previous results (Boyaci et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Rogozina et al., 2009; Suh et al., 1993; Helmann and deHaseth, 1999; Lim et al., 2001; Auner et al., 2003), indicating that promoter unwinding proceeds in a step-wise fashion, in an upstream-downstream direction
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data in this study and by citations to previous results (Boyaci et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Rogozina et al., 2009; Suh et al., 1993; Helmann and deHaseth, 1999; Lim et al., 2001; Auner et al., 2003).

claim: The step for upstream unwinding is slower than downstream unwinding for lacCONS (~5.5 s vs. ~2.0 s).
source: and suggest that the step for upstream unwinding is slower than downstream unwinding for lacCONS (~5.5 s vs. ~2.0 s), whereas the step for downstream unwinding is slower than upstream unwinding for G/C lacCONS (~6.0 s vs. ~13.0 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The step for downstream unwinding is slower than upstream unwinding for G/C lacCONS (~6.0 s vs. ~13.0 s).
source: and suggest that the step for upstream unwinding is slower than downstream unwinding for lacCONS (~5.5 s vs. ~2.0 s), whereas the step for downstream unwinding is slower than upstream unwinding for G/C lacCONS (~6.0 s vs. ~13.0 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Myxopyronin (Myx) is an RNAP inhibitor that prevents RNAP clamp opening.
source: To determine whether promoter unwinding is affected by preventing opening of the RNAP clamp, we repeated our experiments in presence of myxopyronin (Myx; Chakraborty et al., 2012; Feklistov et al., 2017; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Dulin et al., 2018), an RNAP inhibitor that prevents RNAP clamp opening (Chakraborty et al., 2012; Duchi et al., 2018; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; state with an smFRET efficiency, E*~0.36 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chakraborty et al., 2012; Duchi et al., 2018; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008) and by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Myx allows formation of heparin-sensitive RNAP-promoter complexes but prevents formation of heparin-resistant RNAP-promoter complexes.
source: and that allows formation of heparin-sensitive RNAP-promoter complexes but prevents formation of heparin-resistant RNAP-promoter complexes (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B, ).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008) and by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: In the presence of Myx, lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] showed a fluorescence intensity enhancement of ~2.4-fold, consistent with unwinding of the downstream edge of the transcription bubble.
source: We first performed smUIFE experiments in the presence of Myx using promoter DNA fragment lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3], which has Cy3 incorporated at the downstream edge of the transcription bubble. The results showed a fluorescence intensity enhancement of ~2.4-fold, consistent with unwinding of the downstream edge of the transcription bubble (Figure 2B, bottom; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; see Feklistov et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, and by a citation to prior work (Feklistov et al., 2017).

claim: In the presence of Myx, lacCONS-[+ 2 Cy3] showed a dwell time between initial binding and intensity enhancement of ~4.1 s.
source: and showed a dwell time between initial binding and intensity enhancement of ~4.1 s (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of Myx, lacCONS-[–9 Cy3] showed a fluorescence intensity enhancement of ~2.4-fold.
source: We next performed smUIFE experiments in the presence of Myx using promoter DNA fragment lacCONS-[–9 Cy3], which has Cy3 incorporated in the upstream half of the transcription bubble. The results were essentially identical: a fluorescence intensity enhancement of ~2.4-fold (Figure 2B, top; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, top)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the presence of Myx, lacCONS-[–9 Cy3] showed a dwell time between initial binding and intensity enhancement of ~4.0 s.
source: and a dwell time between initial binding and intensity enhancement of ~4.0 s (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed fluorescence intensity enhancements were similar in the absence and presence of Myx.
source: For both promoter derivatives, the observed fluorescence intensity enhancements were similar in the absence and presence of Myx (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 vs. Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The observed dwell times between initial binding and intensity enhancement times were shorter in the presence of Myx than in the absence of Myx (~3.5 s shorter for transcription-bubble downstream edge and ~1.5 s shorter for transcription-bubble upstream half).
source: and the observed dwell times between initial binding and intensity enhancement times were shorter – not longer – in the presence of Myx than in the absence of Myx (~3.5 s shorter for transcription-bubble downstream edge and ~1.5 s shorter for transcription-bubble upstream half; Figure 2B–C vs. Figure 1B–C, top panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C and Figure 1B–C.

claim: Myx prevents formation of heparin-resistant open complexes either by preventing loading of unwound DNA into active-centre cleft or by preventing subsequent locking of the RNAP clamp.
source: We suggest that Myx prevents formation of heparin-resistant open complexes either by preventing loading of unwound DNA into active-centre cleft or by preventing subsequent locking of the RNAP clamp.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Preventing RNAP clamp opening does not prevent promoter unwinding, and increases, not decreases, the kinetics of promoter unwinding.
source: We infer – contrary to the models in which clamp opening is obligatory for promoter unwinding – that preventing RNAP clamp opening does not prevent promoter unwinding, and increases, not decreases, the kinetics of promoter unwinding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing promoter unwinding in the presence of Myx.

claim: Doubly labelled RNAP molecules bound exclusively to immobilised promoter DNA molecules.
source: Control experiments show that: (i) doubly labelled RNAP molecules bound exclusively to immobilised promoter DNA molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority (~87%) of RNAP-promoter complexes formed with doubly labelled RNAP were resistant to challenge with heparin.
source: (ii) the majority (~87%) of the resulting complexes were resistant to challenge with heparin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Doubly labelled RNAP molecules did not bind stably to immobilised non-promoter DNA molecules.
source: (iii) doubly labelled RNAP molecules did not bind stably to immobilised non-promoter DNA molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Sequence-specific, heparin-resistant RNAP-promoter complexes were only formed between the doubly labelled RNAP holoenzyme molecules and promoter DNA fragments.
source: These results indicate that sequence-specific, heparin-resistant RNAP-promoter complexes were only formed between the doubly labelled RNAP holoenzyme molecules and promoter DNA fragments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the control experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The initial binding of RNAP to promoter DNA involved RNAP with a closed clamp (mean E* of ~0.4).
source: In order to determine the RNAP clamp conformations immediately upon initial binding of RNAP to promoter DNA, we plotted distributions of E* values for the first five frames (0.5 s) after initial binding. The resulting distributions could be fitted to a Gaussian function with mean E* of ~0.4, indicating that the initial binding of RNAP to promoter DNA involved RNAP with a closed clamp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No E* changes potentially consistent with clamp opening (E* of ~0.2) were detected in full E* time trajectories following initial binding.
source: Next, we examined full E* time trajectories, for up to ~60 s, following initial binding, seeking E* changes potentially consistent with RNAP clamp opening. We detected no E* changes – not even transient E* changes, within the ~100 ms temporal resolution of the analysis – that potentially could be assigned as consistent with clamp opening (E* of ~0.2; Figure 3B, area highlighted in cyan; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A large fraction of trajectories (~44%) started at E*~0.40, then transitioned to E*~0.48, and then returned to E*~0.40 or photobleached.
source: Intriguingly, a large fraction of trajectories (~44%) started at E*~0.40, indicative of the previously defined closed-clamp state, then transitioned to E*~0.48, indicative of a new, more tightly closed, clamp state, and then returned to E*~0.40 or photobleached (Figure 3B–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The new, more tightly closed, clamp state with E*~0.48 is referred to as the 'locked-clamp' state.
source: We refer to the new, more tightly closed, clamp state with E*~0.48, as the 'locked-clamp' state.
evidence: The claim is a definition based on the experimental observations.

claim: The time between initial binding of RNAP to promoter DNA and appearance of the locked-clamp state was ~7.8 s.
source: We further analysed E* time trajectories to determine the time between initial binding of RNAP to promoter DNA and appearance of the locked-clamp state. The corresponding dwell-time histogram showed a peaked distribution and was fitted to a two-exponential function, yielding ~7.8 s, as the time between initial binding of RNAP to promoter DNA and appearance of the locked-clamp state (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The time between initial binding and appearance of the locked-clamp state (~7.8 s) is, within error, identical to the ~7.5 s time between initial binding and unwinding of the downstream half of the transcription bubble.
source: a time that, within error, is identical to the ~7.5 s time between initial binding and unwinding of the downstream half of the transcription bubble.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of the experimental data for clamp locking and promoter unwinding.

claim: For G/C lacCONS, initial binding by RNAP occurred with a closed-clamp state (E*~0.41).
source: Analogous experiments with a promoter derivative having G/C-rich sequence at positions –4 to +1 relative to the transcription start site, G/C lacCONS, yielded similar results: that is, initial binding by RNAP with a closed-clamp state (E*~0.41; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A; B, left)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: For G/C lacCONS, no trajectories showed transitions to an open-clamp state during a period up to ~200 s after initial binding.
source: no trajectories showing transitions – not even transient transitions, within the ~400 ms temporal resolution of the analysis – to an open-clamp state during a period up to ~200 s after initial binding
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data for G/C lacCONS.

claim: For G/C lacCONS, a large fraction of trajectories (~48%) showed a transition to a locked-clamped state (E*~0.50).
source: a large fraction of trajectories (~48%), showing a transition to a locked-clamped state (E*~0.50, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A; B, right)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: For G/C lacCONS, the time between initial binding and appearance of the locked-clamped state matches the time required for unwinding of the downstream half of the transcription bubble.
source: and a time between initial binding and appearance of the locked-clamped state matching the time required for unwinding of the downstream half of the transcription bubble (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The RNAP clamp is in a closed state upon promoter binding.
source: We conclude that the RNAP clamp is in a closed state upon promoter binding, that the RNAP clamp does not open--not even transiently, within the temporal resolution of our analysis – between promoter binding and promoter unwinding, and that the RNAP clamp closes further – 'locks' – after promoter unwinding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing closed clamp upon binding.

claim: The RNAP clamp does not open--not even transiently, within the temporal resolution of the analysis – between promoter binding and promoter unwinding.
source: We conclude that the RNAP clamp is in a closed state upon promoter binding, that the RNAP clamp does not open--not even transiently, within the temporal resolution of our analysis – between promoter binding and promoter unwinding, and that the RNAP clamp closes further – 'locks' – after promoter unwinding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing no clamp opening events.

claim: The RNAP clamp closes further – 'locks' – after promoter unwinding.
source: We conclude that the RNAP clamp is in a closed state upon promoter binding, that the RNAP clamp does not open--not even transiently, within the temporal resolution of our analysis – between promoter binding and promoter unwinding, and that the RNAP clamp closes further – 'locks' – after promoter unwinding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing transition to a locked-clamp state after unwinding.

claim: RPo formation by E. coli RNAP σ70 holoenzyme at a consensus bacterial core promoter proceeds through a 'bind-unwind-load-and-lock' mechanism.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that RPo formation by E. coli RNAP σ70 holoenzyme at a consensus bacterial core promoter proceeds through a 'bind-unwind-load-and-lock' mechanism, in which the RNAP clamp is closed upon promoter binding, remains closed during unwinding of promoter DNA – which proceeds in an upstream-to-downstream direction – and then closes further, locking the unwound DNA in the RNAP active-centre cleft (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental results and is illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: The finding that the RNAP clamp remains closed throughout promoter unwinding at a consensus bacterial promoter implies that it is ssDNA, not dsDNA, that enters the RNAP active-centre-cleft.
source: Under that predominant view, our finding that the RNAP clamp remains closed throughout promoter unwinding at a consensus bacterial promoter implies that it is ssDNA, not dsDNA, that enters the RNAP active-centre-cleft, and thus that promoter unwinding occurs at least in part outside, not inside, the RNAP active-centre cleft (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and structural considerations.

claim: Promoter unwinding occurs at least in part outside, not inside, the RNAP active-centre cleft.
source: Under that predominant view, our finding that the RNAP clamp remains closed throughout promoter unwinding at a consensus bacterial promoter implies that it is ssDNA, not dsDNA, that enters the RNAP active-centre-cleft, and thus that promoter unwinding occurs at least in part outside, not inside, the RNAP active-centre cleft (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and structural considerations.

claim: The consensus bacterial promoter employed in this study has been used in previous work to define transcription mechanisms.
source: The consensus bacterial promoter employed in this study has been used in previous work to define transcription mechanisms, including RNAP clamp closure upon RPo formation (Chakraborty et al., 2012), DNA scrunching in transcription-start-site selection (Winkelman et al., 2016), DNA scrunching in initial transcription (Kapanidis et al., 2006), and RNAP pausing in initial transcription (Duchi et al., 2016; Winkelman et al., 2020), all of which subsequently were validated for other promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chakraborty et al., 2012; Winkelman et al., 2016; Kapanidis et al., 2006; Duchi et al., 2016; Winkelman et al., 2020).

claim: A recent cryo-EM study of transcription initiation by E. coli RNAP σ70 holoenzyme at the rpsT P2 promoter identified structural states having a partly unwound transcription bubble and a closed RNAP clamp.
source: Consistent with the possibility that a similar mechanism is used by E. coli RNAP σ70 holoenzyme at other promoters, a recent cryo-EM study of transcription initiation by E. coli RNAP σ70 holoenzyme at another promoter, rpsT P2, identified structural states having a partly unwound transcription bubble and a closed RNAP clamp (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a cryo-EM study (Chen et al., 2020).

claim: The smUIFE and smFRET methods reported in this work could be applied to analyse transcription initiation by any E. coli RNAP holoenzyme at any promoter.
source: We note that the smUIFE and smFRET methods reported in this work could be applied to analyse transcription initiation by any E. coli RNAP holoenzyme at any promoter and potentially could be adapted to analyse transcription initiation by any RNAP – bacterial, archaeal, or eukaryotic – at any promoter.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applicability of the methods.
